extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics; architects, sculptors, painters, and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria for evaluating and producing architecture, sculpture, and painting based on classical-aesthetic theory (focus on support/burden, form, proportion, expression, and fidelity to nature). Targets architects and visual artists seeking classical taste and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture's fundamental theme: support and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The one constant theme of architecture is 'support and burden' and its fundamental law is that no burden shall be without sufficient support, and no support without a suitable burden; the relation of these two shall be exactly the fitting one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic effect arises from the clear separation of support and burden (e.g., column and entablature). Even plain walls contain support and burden but fused together produce no aesthetic effect. Use columns, pilasters, or even painted indications of an order to express this separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of support and burden produces aesthetic clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete separation of support (column) and burden (entablature) makes the reciprocal action apparent and yields the purest aesthetic example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer colonnades to plain walls. Intermediate treatments (windows, doors with projecting pilasters) may indicate separation. Avoid designs that fuse support and burden (e.g., vaulting that makes every stone both burden and support) when the intent is the classical aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaulting and arches fuse support and burden (less classical aesthetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaults and some arches fuse support and burden because each part is both burden and support, therefore they do not attain the same aesthetic effect as the column-entablature system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that vaults have different aesthetic character; structural necessities (lateral thrust) demand massive piers rather than slender columns. Do not simply substitute columns where vaulting requires solid piers; appreciate the differing aesthetic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supports should show ample superfluity without excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The support is not adapted to the burden when it is only sufficient; it should appear so convenient and ample that we are at ease about it, but this superfluity must not exceed a certain degree to avoid perceiving support without burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancients achieved this via line of equilibrium and entasis (slight swelling). Anti-pattern: balconies or projections that seem to hang unsupported and thus disturb the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of entasis and line of equilibrium in column design
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancients devised a line of equilibrium by diminishing column thickness upward and using a slight increase (entasis) where pressure is greatest, so cross sections leave the lower part able to support upper cut-off parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply entasis subtly to avoid visual discord; adhere to proportions determined by structural end. Avoid arbitrary or decorative swelling that lacks structural justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of the column determined a priori by structural ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the column has its sole ground in that it affords the simplest and most suitable support; all proportions and details follow from the relation of necessary support to given burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on accidental models (trees, human form). Twisted columns are inappropropriate and condemned by good taste; round columns are exclusive natural solution, with polygonal (hex/octagon) acceptable as approximations; four-cornered pillars are less pleasing because diagonals exceed sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column proportions and spacing must match load and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of thickness to height, relation to intervals between columns, and relation of series to entablature result from calculating adequate support for a uniformly distributed burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose Doric or heavier orders for larger burdens (thicker columns, closer spacing). Groups of columns are tasteless because support must be uniformly distributed; corner columns may be placed slightly closer to account for increased burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals should visibly express bearing function
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals serve to show visibly that columns bear the entablature and increase bearing surface by their abacus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design capitals to make structural function obvious; avoid ornamental capitals that obscure bearing function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture favors regular forms and easily comprehensible proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful architecture selects regular figures (straight lines, regular curves) and solids (cubes, cylinders, spheres, pyramids, cones), openings usually quadrate/rectangular with comprehensible ratios (e.g., 1:2, 2:3), not awkward ratios like 6:7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple numerical ratios and regular geometry in façades and openings. Use blind windows or niches of regular proportions. Anti-pattern: capricious, irregular proportions that impede quick perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building size and mass are essential to aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture, in order to act aesthetically, absolutely must have considerable size; the aesthetic effect is in exact proportion to the size of the building because great masses make the action of gravitation apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceteris paribus, larger masses produce stronger aesthetic impact. Smallness undermines the visibility of the 'fundamental forces' architecture expresses (gravity vs rigidity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of perception and surveyability (clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture appeals to our a priori faculty for spatial perception; therefore it must present the clearest forms and relations for easiest comprehensibility and be easily surveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce symmetry (subordinate to structural relations) to mark the work as a whole and distinguish essential from accidental parts. Use rational and regular placement so a viewer can apprehend the whole at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry is subordinate to structural truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural relations (relations between support and burden) are the essential ones, to which symmetry, as subordinate, must give way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit deviations from strict symmetry when structural necessity or load distribution requires it (e.g., corner column spacing). Do not sacralize symmetry over sound structural expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should work in the spirit of nature (avoid aimless ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture ought to work in the spirit of nature and avoid everything apparently aimless; it attains ends by the shortest and most natural path and thus openly exhibits ends through the work itself, producing grace analogous to nature's fitness of parts to ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor naive simplicity and direct attainment of ends. Anti-patterns include aimless broken entablatures, grouped columns, fragmentary cornices, meaningless volutes and scrolls—forms of the bungler who plays with tools without understanding aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical (antique) style as normative for fine-art architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: For the fine-art part of architecture the classical (antique) style, especially Greek, is essentially determinate and not susceptible of important enrichment; modern architects must apply ancient rules within local limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits to innovation in the purely aesthetic domain—improvements are mainly in wise application rather than novel invention. Treat Gothic as a different spirit (subjective) rather than an equal replacement for antique style when the classical aesthetic is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic expresses a different fundamental idea (conquest of gravity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic architecture's fundamental thought is the supposed overcoming and conquest of gravity by rigidity: horizontal line (burden) vanishes and vertical support predominates, producing a hyperphysical, mysterious character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand Gothic as a contrasting, more subjective mode; its interior (groined vaulting on slender pillars) has strong effect, but exterior often lacks the classical rationality. Use historically or associatively rather than claiming parity with antique objective spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture prioritizes beauty, grace, strength and fullness
rubrics_metrics.description: In sculpture beauty and grace are principal; sculpture demands strength and fullness of figures rather than emaciation; perfect bodily beauty is required to avoid monotony from excessive characterisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid emaciated or excessively attenuated figures in sculpture (even if masterly executed these may be repulsive). Classical proportions and the full-bodied type are preferable for sculptural beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting prioritizes expression, passion, and character over pure beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting, expression, passion, and character predominate, so painting may neglect some claims of beauty; it may portray ugly or emaciated figures where appropriate for expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept departures from sculptural ideals where dramatic or narrative expression requires it (e.g., dying figures, tragic expressions). Balance expressive aims with subordinate pictorial beauties (color harmony, composition, light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting's subordinate beauty: color harmony and tonal composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides making Ideas more comprehensible, painting has an independent subordinate beauty produced by harmony of colours, pleasing grouping, distribution of light and shade, and the tone of the whole picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color, grouping, and chiaroscuro to further the cognitive/aesthetic aim. These are analogous to diction and metre in poetry—secondary but immediately effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory is inadmissible or problematic in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory in painting is often inadmissible because pictorial hieroglyphs may be unintelligible to those without prior knowledge; allegorical symbolism that requires learned associations fails as visual art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure or learned allegory that cannot be apprehended visually. Examples given: Caravaggio's Christ treading on a serpent or elaborate ceiling allegories that depend on prior scriptural or scholarly knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint from living models and prefer portraits in historical painting
rubrics_metrics.description: In historical paintings only real portraits should figure; invented faces are suspect because an imagined face may be an impossible or incoherent physiognomic unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should paint from living models and introduce portraits. When inventing faces, idealise with extreme care; prefer actual, observed physiognomies to conjured composites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of sound (shrieking) is faulty in visual arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The plastic and pictorial arts are essentially dumb; attempts to represent shrieking (wide-open mouths) produce a faulty, comic, or absurd effect rather than the intended solemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid depicting auditory phenomena (shriek, loud speech) by static visual cues that cannot convey sound; the example of Guido Reni's slaughter-of-the-innocents with many wide-open mouths is given as a mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic anticipation (a priori ideal) needs empirical refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery and retention of the type of human beauty depends in part on an a priori anticipation but this anticipation requires experience to be stirred and determined in its details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists and poets should cultivate experience (observation of living forms) to refine innate artistic anticipation—e.g., Greek sculptors benefited from constant exposure to nude bodies in gymnasia to form ideal types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skill in painting: separate sensation from cause to recreate perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter's craft is to separate in seeing the mere sensation (retinal affection) from its ordinary cause (external world) and, by applied colour patches, produce the same effect so the viewer's understanding reconstructs the ordinary perception from a different cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop technique that convinces the eye/understanding (colour, brushwork) to elicit intended perception; this is a technical rather than purely intellectual accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern imitation vs classical originality warning
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern sculpture and much modern art are likened to the children of imitation and reminiscence; if modern artists attempt originality by following nature as it lies before them they often go astray instead of following classical proportions and ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value classical patterns and proportions; modern originality that departs from classical taste often results in poor taste. Apply ancient methods where the classical aesthetic is the goal, and recognise the limits of novelty in fine art domains.
